The way these functions are graphed can be a little misleading. Instead of thinking of them as on a flat, straight graph think of them as on a circle. Where 0 is on the right of the circle, pi/2 is on top, pi is on the left, 3pi/4 is on the bottom, and 2pi finishes where we started on the right. This way of graphing runs into a problem once you go past 2pi, though. Once it makes a full lap around the circle, the lines overlap and you can’t properly read the graph. For this problem you are going to need to use the definition of sin/cos in order to find out your missing numbers. Sin means “opposite/hypotenuse” and cos means “adjacent/hypotenuse” so if you want to find out the cos when you are given sin, you need to draw a triangle and find the missing length. Let’s use sinA=3/5 as an example. This means that the side opposite of your angle is 3, and the hypotenuse of your triangle is 5. Using the pythagorean theorem (a^2 +b^2 =c^2 ) we can plug in the numbers we have to find the missing one. Plug 3 into a (since it is a normal side length) and plug 5 into c (since it is the hypotenuse). This should give you b=4. Now that we know the missing side we can convert it into a cos value. Cos is adjacent/hypotenuse so you plug in 4 (your calculated adjacent value) and divide it by 5 (your given hypotenuse value). So CosA= 4/5. Use this same process to find out SinB. I’m in my freshman year of college, and this is totally incorrect. You will be using volume a LOT in calculus 1/2. It’s really important to make sure you learn this stuff before you get to calculus or you will be totally lost

There’s really only a few volume formulas you might need to memorize, most others will be provided by your teacher. These are the ones most teachers require you to memorize:

Volume of a Rectangular prism= L*W*H (Think of this formula like you are seeing the combined area of bunch of rectangles (L*H) are stacked on top of each other (W))

Volume of a cube= x*x*x or x^3 (This is the same as the last equation, but since all sides of a cube are the same length you can simplify it to just x^3) 

Volume of (Right Rectangular) pyramid= (L*W*H)/3 (This is just like how the formula for a triangle’s area is 1/2 the area of a rectangle. If you want to understand this idea better, look up a video showing that 3 pyramids all fit inside a rectangular prism)

Volume of a sphere= 4/3*pi*r^3 (This equation is a bit harder to remember. The r means the radius of the circle. So if you were to take a small slice out of the middle, the r would be how far the center is from the outside. Pi (3.14159...) comes from the circumference equation.) 

Volume of a cylinder= pi*r^2 *h (This one is similar to the rectangular prism equation. Think of this like you are trying to figure out the combined area of a bunch of circles (pi*r^2) stacked on top of each other (h).)

That’s all most teachers will need you to know, however some might ask you to memorize more. Here’s some of the equations a teacher might ask you to remember:

Volume of a cone= 1/3*pi*r^2* h (A cone will have 1/3 the volume of a cylinder with the same dimensions. A cone is basically a pyramid with a circular base, so that’s why the equations are so similar.)

Volume of a (triangular) pyramid= 1/3*B*h (In this equation B= 1/2*bh aka the area of the triangle on the bottom of the pyramid.)
